lesson.title: The Bloodiest Single Day: Antietam and Lee's First Invasion Repelled
lesson.summary: On September 17, 1862, Union and Confederate armies clashed near Sharpsburg, Maryland in the single bloodiest day in American military history, a tactical draw that nonetheless stopped Robert E. Lee's first invasion of the North and gave Lincoln the opening he needed for the Emancipation Proclamation.
lesson.body:
By the late summer of 1862, the Union's broader strategy of blockade and gradual pressure, embodied in Winfield Scott's earlier Anaconda Plan, had not produced the quick, dramatic victory many Northerners still hoped for, and Confederate General Robert E. Lee decided to seize the initiative. Fresh off a victory at the Second Battle of Bull Run, Lee led the Army of Northern Virginia across the Potomac River into Maryland in early September 1862, hoping a successful invasion of Union territory might win diplomatic recognition from Britain or France, encourage anti-war sentiment in the North, and possibly pull the border state of Maryland toward the Confederacy.

Lee's plan nearly fell apart before the battle even began. A copy of his detailed marching orders, known as Special Order 191, was lost and then found wrapped around a bundle of cigars by Union soldiers, giving Union commander George McClellan a rare look at exactly where Lee's divided forces were headed. Even with this advantage, McClellan, a famously cautious general, moved slowly enough that Lee had time to reconsolidate much of his army near the town of Sharpsburg, Maryland, along a creek called Antietam. The two armies met there on September 17, 1862, in fighting that raged across cornfields, a sunken farm road that soldiers afterward called Bloody Lane, and a stone bridge over the creek that Union troops struggled for hours to cross under fire.

The single day of fighting produced roughly 22,000 combined casualties, killed, wounded, and missing, making it the bloodiest day in American history, a toll never matched even by the deadliest days at Gettysburg the following year. Neither side could claim a clean tactical victory; Lee's army held its ground through the day's fighting but was too battered and outnumbered to continue, and on September 18 he withdrew his forces back across the Potomac into Virginia. McClellan, with fresh reserves still uncommitted, chose not to pursue aggressively, a decision that frustrated Lincoln and eventually contributed to McClellan's removal from command later that year.

Strategically, Antietam mattered enormously. Lee's invasion had been turned back, and the Confederacy's best chance yet at winning European recognition evaporated once it became clear the Army of Northern Virginia could not sustain an offensive on Union soil. Just as important, the outcome gave Lincoln the battlefield success he had been waiting for to announce a major shift in the war's purpose. Five days later, on September 22, 1862, Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, warning that enslaved people in any state still in rebellion on January 1, 1863 would be declared free, turning a war originally fought to preserve the Union into one that would also mean the end of slavery.
